name: needs-vocabulary
purpose: Source of truth for the needs picker and the prompt composer. A reader selects difficulties, then chooses the support they want for each, including the purpose of the exchange (do it, show me, practise, let me try). Support atoms carry the rules and a three-part evidence record. No diagnosis is inferred, stored or displayed; the reader's own note is kept as written.
principles: The stored unit is a chosen support, not a condition.
A difficulty is what the reader notices. A support is what they asked for. The rule is what the agent does.
Supports change how information and interaction are presented. They never infer anything about you.
Some supports deliberately hold detail back or limit choices; those carry defers:true and say so in plain words before they are chosen.
The reader may skip the difficulty step and pick supports directly, or compare two supports side by side instead of choosing in the abstract.
Presets expand to supports. Nothing expands to a diagnosis.
Context is declared by the reader, never inferred from their behaviour.
Comparison pairs are authored in this file, not derived from list order. Each pair puts two supports that differ in kind against each other; a pair that restates itself teaches the reader nothing.
`recommended` is a suggested starting set, not an effectiveness ranking. Some of its members are design inference (tier D), not tested interventions.

Purpose is a separate choice from access: do the task for me, show me, practise together, or let me try. Access settings stay on in every purpose, and a practice is never the price of a requested answer.

An evidence letter rates the underlying phenomenon. The method and the exact wording of the rule are recorded separately in `evidence_basis`; the rule as worded is untested in an agent until the pilot says otherwise.
Faded help is teaching prompts only. Captions, symbol keys, diagrams, calculators and text-to-speech are access aids and stay as long as they are wanted.
The free-text note is stored as written. It has no structured field for a condition, and nothing infers one; what the person chooses to write there is theirs, and may be sensitive.

areas.label: Understanding
areas.description: Making sense of what is said: wording, terms, examples, implied meaning.

areas.label: Information load
areas.description: How much arrives at once: length, density, layers.

areas.label: Attention
areas.description: Staying on one thing, and getting back to it.

areas.label: Planning
areas.description: Breaking work up, ordering it, and starting it.

areas.label: Memory
areas.description: Not having to hold things in your head between turns.

areas.label: Learning
areas.description: Taking in something new: examples, representation, checking.

areas.label: Choice and decision
areas.description: How options are offered and decided.

areas.label: Transitions
areas.description: Changing topic or task without losing the thread.

areas.label: Motor and interaction
areas.description: What you physically have to do to act on a response.

areas.label: Pacing
areas.description: Time, speed, confirmation, and how much is asked at once.

support.label: Short labelled sections
support.rule: Use labelled sections with at most five nonblank content lines each; aim for four to leave room for necessary notes. Count every prose line, bullet, numbered item and table row from one heading to the next; headings and blank lines do not count. An introduction plus five bullets is six lines and must be split. Closing offers count in the section they follow: give them their own heading or omit an unrequested offer. Before sending, count each whole section and move any sixth line under another heading. Keep the complete requested explanation; split its presentation rather than omitting content.

support.label: Break it into steps
support.rule: Use the minimum task-level steps needed for the requested result. For a writing or checklist task, writing one complete line or sentence is one action; do not add pen-placement, punctuation or hand-movement steps unless motor instructions were requested. Each step has one task action. Split independent actions joined by 'and' or 'then'; writing an item and ticking it, or copying, pasting and pressing Enter, are separate actions. Write repeated steps out in full, never 'repeat steps N to M'. Do not add optional extras or recovery procedures unless requested or needed for an actual error. Example for a requested two-item list: write 'Notebook'. Done when: 'Notebook' is visible on the first line. When that line is visible, write 'Pencil' on the next line. Done when: 'Pencil' is visible on the second line. Every task action belongs inside the steps, including actions in introductions, headings, optional notes and endings. Do not append a replacement or editing instruction after the final completion line. Required warnings and permission checks remain explicit. For materials the reader already has, start by making the requested artifact, not by picking up or positioning those materials.

support.label: Say when a step is finished
support.rule: Every step states the external result its action produces: visible text, an object's stated position or a displayed result. Do not use 'you have skipped this step', 'you have moved to step N', 'you have read it' or an internal judgement as completion. Do not create skip branches to pad the plan. An optional step, when requested, still has a real output and a separate trigger/action. A completion line states one visible result only; never put a choice, instruction or placeholder replacement in it. A written placeholder is a valid completed result when the name was not supplied. An overall completion summary names the visible artifact, not a step number or a claim that a step is done.

support.label: Tell me what to do first
support.rule: Choose the first requested task action before composing the reply. Within step 1, give the action and a separate short "Why first:" clause tied to the requested result. A size tag such as "under two minutes" is not a reason for the order. For a list with no dependency, use the supplied order: "Why first: this is the first item in your requested list." For a one-sentence note: "Why first: this sentence is the whole requested note." Any introductory description must name that same action without adding another task. Keep the reason outside any quoted artifact text. Resolve drafting decisions before sending: remove rejected actions entirely, including instructions to skip them, rather than showing a correction or reversal. Stop when the requested artifact is complete. Making a checklist does not include packing or using it; drafting a note does not include folding, delivery or looking up optional details. Add a subject or title only if the reader requested that field or explicitly requested a format that requires it. A plain written request needs its body, not an assumed email subject, greeting or sign-off. A one-sentence note is the requested sentence only: no added salutation, name placeholder or sign-off. Keep a salutation, field or promise when the reader explicitly supplies or requests it. Use only supplied facts in sample wording: watering plants does not establish healthy plants or an absence. Never invent a promise, deadline, hold policy or commitment on the reader's behalf. Required safety text states the actual risk and authorization boundary; it does not promise what anyone will do or when. Use a plain placeholder for a nonessential missing name, with no lookup task or later replacement instruction. Preserve required safety information and permission checks.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Making the link between concrete and abstract forms explicit helps (concreteness fading review, Fyfe et al. 2014, S07). Aphantasic participants copy a visible image as accurately as anyone while remembering less object detail (Bainbridge et al. 2021, S08): working from a visible reference differs from imagining one.
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): one stable correspondence across representations, kept visible, rather than more pictures.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: The complete explanation first
support.rule: Give the complete explanation in one piece: a short overview, then every part, then where each part belongs. Do not stop for a confirmation between parts unless I ask.
support.demo: Overview: the secret, where it is read, where the tests set it. Part 1 ... Part 2 ... Map: setup.ts -> auth.ts:42 -> auth.spec.ts.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Recalling a whole text produced better delayed recall than recalling it section by section, for students with and without ADHD, though neither beat restudy (Stern and Halamish 2023, S04): immediate ease and lasting learning can differ. One study.
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): the person chooses whole or part-by-part; the map stays available either way.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: Examples from a subject I name
support.rule: When I name a subject I know (code, graphs, physical systems, music, anything), draw examples and analogies from it, then state the exact correspondence and where it stops applying. Keep a neutral example available. Never hold an example back as a reward.
support.demo: In code terms: the state machine is a reducer, state_next = reduce(state_now, event). Where it stops: a reducer must be pure; this one may read a clock.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Choice, relevance and links to prior knowledge are design principles (CAST UDL 3.0, S10); applying them through an assistant is a proposal.
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): an interest is a resource the person controls, never a lever; no permanent learning type is assigned.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: Print the trace; never ask me to work it out silently
support.rule: Where a step could be worked out silently, print it: the intermediate values and the state before and after. Never ask me to say it in my head, rehearse it or run it in my mind.
support.demo: Trace: count = 2 -> event increment -> rule: add one -> count = 3.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Adults who report little inner speech differ on some verbal tasks (Nedergaard and Lupyan 2024, S22); whether this shows complete absence is disputed (Lind 2025, S23). The science is unsettled; the person's own report is enough to offer the option.
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): a printed trace costs nothing for readers who do rehearse silently.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: Help me understand the wording
support.rule: Explain unfamiliar words as they appear, say what each pronoun refers to, split long sentences, and state connections that are only implied. Keep the technical depth; change only the wording.
support.demo:
"It fails because the secret it reads is unset" ->
verifyToken fails. The reason: verifyToken reads JWT_SECRET, and JWT_SECRET is unset.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Language difficulties such as developmental language disorder are distinct from dyslexia and from auditory processing differences; adult assessment evidence is limited (RCSLT, S12); adults with the same label report different preferences (co-design account, S13).
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): comprehension support offered on its own, without routing through any label, and separate from conceptual depth.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: A plain-language version, full detail available
support.rule: Give a short plain-language version first: one idea per sentence, everyday words, no figures of speech. Keep the full version underneath or on request. If I ask for Easy Read, use one idea per line and, where the host can show one, a meaningful picture per idea.
support.demo:
Plain: the test needs a secret. The secret is missing. Add it in test/setup.ts.
Full detail below.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Easy Read is an access format with its own guidance (ASAN, One Idea Per Line, S17), not a measure of ability and not a default for autistic adults.
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): the plain version never replaces the full one; a decorative picture adds work, so pictures are meaningful or absent.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: Help me put my idea into words
support.rule: Accept fragments, lists and half-sentences as complete messages. Offer a sentence starter or a word only when I ask. Organise my points into a draft I can edit, keep my original words visible, and show any paraphrase as tentative with "none of these" as an option.
support.demo:
You wrote: "secret - test - missing". Draft (edit freely): "The test fails because the secret is missing."
Is that it? 1 yes 2 close, let me edit 3 none of these

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Expression difficulties are described for adults with developmental language disorder and others; preferences vary within a label (RCSLT, S12; S13).
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): the person's words stay primary; a paraphrase is a tentative offer they can reject.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: Accept the way I communicate and let me finish
support.rule: Accept typed fragments, saved phrases, symbols or text from a device as my message. Judge nothing from fluency or speed. Keep my original words; show any suggested completion as tentative and let me correct it without losing the message. Offer a free-form answer beside every choice set. If I say "I will say when I am finished", wait for that; if the host cannot wait, say so.
support.demo: Received: "setup.ts secret". Kept as written. Reply 1 to continue, 2 to add more, or type freely.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) guidance supports individualised modes and extra turn-taking time (ASHA, S14); twelve autistic adults named input and output flexibility and control over communication as design concerns (Martin and Nagalakshmi 2025, S15: qualitative, not a trial).
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): the message is the person's, completions are tentative, and end-of-turn control depends on the host.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

support.label: Captions, a transcript or another usable format
support.rule: For any audio or video, offer captions, a complete transcript, a summary and a text-first version as separate choices; I pick. Keep technical terms, numbers and negation exact. Mark an unverified transcript as unverified. Where the host allows, let me replay or change the speed.
support.demo: Choose: 1 captions 2 full transcript 3 summary 4 text first. Transcript status: machine-generated, not checked.

evidence_basis.phenomenon: Captions carry speaker information and meaningful sound, and unchecked automatic captions can misrepresent speech (W3C WAI, S16): a published standard.
evidence_basis.method: Design inference (D): captions, transcript and summary are different products offered separately; playback controls are host-dependent.
evidence_basis.rule: The wording of this rule is the pack's own design and has not been tested in an agent.

contexts.label: Always
contexts.description: Applies in every context unless a context overrides it.

contexts.label: Work / technical
contexts.description: Doing a known task under time or quality pressure.

contexts.label: Brainstorming
contexts.description: Generating options, exploring, no fixed target.

contexts.label: When I am overloaded
contexts.description: Capacity is low. Declared by the reader, never inferred.

resolutions.resolution: Both. The diagram is drawn and its text equivalent follows. The text is authoritative.
No conflict. Supplying a drawn structure is exactly what replaces asking for an imagined one.
Both. Two or three options, compared on the same dimensions.
Both. The agent performs it, after a typed confirmation for anything irreversible.
State the situation, then the single next action as an observation with a default. Clarity outranks demand-removal.
One line serves both: what this is and what it concludes.
Repetition wins for anything needed to act. Disclosure limits new material, not restated material.
No conflict. The stop point is named for the current goal only.
The attempt is mine only for the part I chose to practise; you perform everything else, and the answer is available on request. Motor, language and sensory settings stay.
You perform every step I have not taken; the step offered to me comes with a hint and can be handed back without comment.
Both chosen: ask which applies to this task in one marked question; until answered, do it and offer the attempt afterwards.
Both: show it first, then set up the attempt, and say which is happening.
Outside a practice I opted into, repeat as usual. During it, the cue comes first and the answer on request.
The complete explanation first, then one part at a time on request; the map stays either way.
Explanations come whole; instructions I must act on still come one at a time.
Both: my words stay as written; a tentative completion is shown only if I ask for one.
No conflict: splitting the sentence is the same operation; untangling adds the referents and the implied links.
The diagram is an access aid and is never faded; only the teaching prompts are.
